definitions.Verifiable fact: A statement that can be checked and confirmed, often common knowledge.
definitions.Opinion: A judgment or preference. It can be reasonable but cannot be proven true or false.
definitions.Unsupported claim: An assertion presented as true with no evidence offered.
definitions.Credible evidence: Information from an identified, qualified source that you can trace and check.
definitions.Questionable research: Research exists, but something weakens it: tiny sample, conflict of interest, misrepresentation, or no way to trace it.

items.text: "Pizza is the best school lunch option."
items.feedback: This is a preference. You could support it with survey data about what students choose, but the statement itself is a judgment.

items.text: "At sea level, water boils at 100 degrees Celsius."
items.feedback: Widely documented and easy to confirm, so it is common knowledge and usually does not need a citation.

items.text: "Everyone knows phones are destroying our attention spans."
items.feedback: "Everyone knows" replaces evidence. The topic is researchable, but this sentence offers no source.

items.text: "A peer-reviewed study of about 2,000 students, published in a university journal, found this pattern, and two later studies by other researchers found similar results."
items.feedback: Peer review, a substantial sample, and independent replication make this strong. In your speech, name the journal and year.

items.text: "An energy drink company's website reports that 9 out of 10 customers who took its online survey felt more focused."
items.feedback: The company profits from the result, and people who chose to answer may not represent everyone. Look for independent research.

items.text: "According to our county's published crash report for last year, this intersection had more reported crashes than any other in the county."
items.feedback: An identified public source you can trace and check. Go upstream to the report itself if you can.

items.text: "A study of 15 volunteers over one weekend proves that a new study app doubles test scores."
items.feedback: Fifteen people over one weekend is a tiny, short study, and "proves" overstates any single study. Check who funded it.

items.text: "The new library hours are inconvenient for students who work after school."
items.feedback: A reasonable judgment, but still a judgment. You could strengthen it with a survey of working students.
